name: Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail
author: author-E-2026-10-18
summary:
The Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail runs about 3,700 miles to the mouth of the Columbia River near Astoria, Oregon, through 11 states and many tribal lands; the 2012 foundation document places its start at Wood River, Illinois, while the 2016 brochure says Hartford, Illinois. Congress established it in 1978 as one of the four original national historic trails, and the Park Service administers it through partnerships with agencies, tribal nations, nonprofits and private landowners. Along the route are the junction of the Knife and Missouri rivers, where the Corps wintered near the villages of the Mandan and Hidatsa, the Great Falls of the Missouri, Lemhi Pass on the Continental Divide, the Bitterroot Mountains, and Beacon Rock, where Clark saw the first sign of tidal water. [1] [2]

The NPS brochure says the Corps of Discovery would not have reached the Pacific and returned without the help of tribes like the Mandan and Hidatsa, Shoshone, Nez Perce and Clatsop, who provided food, trade, knowledge of the country ahead and guides. In September 1805, near starvation, the party came out of the Bitterroots near today’s Weippe, Idaho, and was fed and cared for by the Nez Perce. Only once, with Piegan Blackfeet in July 1806, did an encounter turn violent; two Blackfeet were killed. [1]

The trail’s 2012 foundation document acknowledges that some call the expedition an epic event leading to a young nation’s growth, while others characterize it as having huge disruptive impacts on rich Indigenous cultures. It says tribal oral histories, with the journals’ descriptions, substantiate, validate and enrich understanding of the tribes the expedition met. [1]

indigenous.html:
The federal government later flooded many of the expedition’s water routes. According to the trail’s 2018 administrative history, fifteen dams rose on the Missouri alone between 1890 and 1963; the Pick-Sloan Plan, approved in 1944, flooded more than 550 square miles of tribal land in North and South Dakota and forced more than 900 American Indian families from their homes. [1]

Many tribes were wary of the expedition’s bicentennial. Superintendent Gerard Baker, who grew up on the Fort Berthold Reservation, promised them they could tell their stories without censorship, edits or curation; historians Jackie Gonzales and Emily Greenwald write that the NPS had a long history of making such promises to tribes that it later broke. In October 2000 Allen Pinkham led the first tribally run planning meeting, at Lewiston, Idaho; eleven tribes there chose to take part, and the Circle of Tribal Advisors grew to about forty tribes, two-thirds of those Lewis and Clark documented. [1]

sources.title: Jackie Gonzales and Emily Greenwald, Commemoration and Collaboration: An Administrative History of the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail (NPS, 2018), pp. 24, 158–162

women.html:
Sacagawea, a 16-year-old Shoshone, joined the Corps at Fort Mandan with her husband, the trapper Toussaint Charbonneau; their son Jean Baptiste, born in February 1805, traveled the whole route. She recognized Beaverhead Rock near her people’s homeland, met her brother Cameahwait, a Shoshone leader, and in November 1805 voted with the Corps on where to winter. [1]

A century later, the administrative history recounts, suffragist Eva Emery Dye’s 1903 novel recast her as a heroine for the women’s suffrage movement, and Dye and other Portland Women’s Club members raised $7,000 for a statue unveiled at Portland’s 1905 Lewis and Clark Centennial Exposition. In 2006 Stephenie Ambrose Tubbs wrote that Sacagawea’s history had been replaced with “almost 80 percent myth, legend, and fantasy,” and that her greater genius would seem to be her memory for landscapes, her skill as a translator and her ability to harvest foods. [1] [2]

slavery.html: York, the brochure says, was a Black man held in slavery by William Clark. A Park Service page, as captured in December 2024, described him as a skilled frontiersman, likely the first African American to cross North America, born into a system that considered him property. His presence, with Sacagawea’s and her baby’s, was a curiosity to the tribes, and in November 1805 he too voted on where to winter. After the return the men received double pay and 320 acres; York, the NPS page said, was denied his payment and his freedom. During the bicentennial, Louisville unveiled a bronze statue of York on its Ohio River waterfront, and living history actor Hasan Davis portrayed him at a 2006 Corps II signature event in New Town, North Dakota. [1] [2] [3]
